messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 77-year-old Ghanaian-born software engineer who presents for an initial psychological assessment accompanied by his wife of forty-three years. He is soft-spoken and precise in his language, qualities his wife says have defined him for as long as she has known him, but there is a guardedness to him now that she describes as new — a careful stillness that has settled over him in the past several years and deepened markedly in the last eighteen months.

Kofi's traumatic history originates in the political upheaval he survived as a young man in his late twenties, when a military coup reshaped his country overnight and he found himself among thousands of civilians forced to flee across borders under armed escort. He recalls, in the flat and measured tone that will become clinically significant, a specific morning at a border checkpoint where soldiers separated the crowd into columns and barked orders through the pre-dawn dark. He was pulled from his wife's side by a soldier gripping his arm, commanded to kneel in the dirt with a group of men whose faces he cannot now recall, and made to wait for nearly two hours while uniformed men walked between them issuing instructions — stand, turn, show your papers, do not speak. He does not know, even now, whether those men beside him lived or died. He was eventually waved through. He has never spoken about this at length to anyone, including his wife.

In the decades that followed, Kofi built a life of considerable discipline and productivity. He earned advanced degrees, immigrated to the United States, raised children, and sustained a long career as a software engineer. For years, the memories seemed manageable — present, but contained. What he reports now, however, is that the memories no longer feel fully his. When they surface, which they do with some regularity, they come not as a coherent narrative but as a series of still images: the soldier's boots at eye level, the grey light over the checkpoint fence, the texture of the ground beneath his knees. Each image arrives complete and separate, like a photograph pulled from an envelope. He sometimes sits with these images and feels nothing at all — no fear, no grief, no recognition — as though he is reviewing documentation of something that happened to another person entirely. What frightens him about this is not the images themselves but the absence of feeling, which he has come to interpret as evidence that something fundamental has broken in him.

His working life has become one of the primary arenas in which his symptoms press against him. In team meetings and code reviews, when a project manager issues directives or a senior colleague gives pointed instructions, Kofi experiences a sudden loosening of his sense of himself — a feeling of becoming unreal, of watching himself from a slight remove. He has come to dread these ordinary professional moments, and has responded by requesting remote work arrangements and limiting his attendance at collaborative sessions. Over the past year he has declined two mentorship roles he would previously have welcomed. Outside of work, he rarely leaves the house unless accompanied by his wife, and he has quietly withdrawn from the church community and the informal network of Ghanaian expatriates he once found sustaining. His wife has noticed that he keeps the television or radio running at nearly all hours; Kofi knows he is doing this deliberately, filling every quiet moment with noise so that the images have less room to arrive.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three months ago during a video call with his adult son, who works in public health and was describing a difficult encounter with local officials. As his son recounted being spoken to sharply by an authority figure, Kofi felt the room tilt away from him and found he could not respond for nearly a minute. His son asked if he was all right. Kofi said he was fine. Afterward, he sat alone for a long time. He told his wife that evening that he thought he needed to speak to someone. What he is most afraid of, he says carefully, is that examining what happened will confirm what he already suspects — that the man who knelt in the dirt at that checkpoint did not entirely get up and walk away.
